new_statements.quote: § 10. Eine bestimmte Regel über die Betonung läßt sich nicht aufstellen. Unter 196 mehrsilbigen Worten waren etwa gleichviel auf der ultima und paenultima betont, 25 auf der antepaenultima. Es geht daraus hervor, daß die Bongu-Sprache die beiden letzten Silben als Träger des Akzentes bevorzugt. Dieselbe Tendenz tritt auch in dem Umstande zutage, daß der Akzent, wenn ein Wort durch ein Suffix verlängert wird, nach dem Ende zu wandert. Z. B.: íṅgĭ, Speise, iṅgĭgā́, für Speise; [...] bagála, Lagerstatt, bagalẹ́ō, auf der Lagerstatt. § 11. Bei geminierten Formen (cf. § 22) bleibt der Akzent in der Regel da, wo ihn das einfache Wort hatte: [...] olé, lang; oléolé, sehr lang.
new_statements.translation: Par.10. No definite rule about stress can be set up. Among 196 polysyllabic words about equally many were stressed on the ultima and on the penult, 25 on the antepenult. It follows that the Bongu language prefers the last two syllables as bearers of the accent. The same tendency also shows in the fact that the accent, when a word is lengthened by a suffix, moves toward the end, e.g. íngi 'food', ingigá 'for food'; bagála 'sleeping place', bagaléo 'on the sleeping place'. Par.11. In reduplicated forms (cf. par.22) the accent as a rule stays where the simple word had it: olé 'long', oléolé 'very long'.
new_statements.citation: Hanke, August. 1909. Grammatik und Vokabularium der Bongu-Sprache (Astrolabebai, Kaiser-Wilhelmsland). (Archiv fuer das Studium deutscher Kolonialsprachen, Band VIII.) Berlin: Druck und Kommissionsverlag von Georg Reimer.
new_statements.locator: Erster Teil: Lautlehre, G. Akzent, par. 10-11, p. 13 (= PDF page 451 of the archive.org item bub_gb_TVdIAQAAMAAJ, Archiv Bd. V-VIII bound together)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not predictable by a single rule: in Hanke's count of 196 polysyllables, final and penultimate stress are about equally common and antepenultimate stress occurs in a minority (25/196), i.e. stress falls within a three-syllable right-edge window with a strong preference for the last two syllables; when case/postpositional suffixes are added the stress shifts rightward onto or toward the suffix; in reduplications each copy keeps the stress of the simplex. Hanke marks stress with an acute on cited forms in the grammar.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (reduplicated forms are cited with an accent on each copy, e.g. oléolé).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress in 25 of 196 polysyllables; stress migrates toward the word end under suffixation (íngi > ingigá, bá'ne > ba'negú, bagála > bagaléo); reduplicated forms keep the simplex stress. Yes/no questions are usually signalled by intonation rather than the particle (p.84, par.145).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns citation forms of polysyllabic words (Hanke's own count over 196 words) and suffixed word forms; the examples with suffixes show the stress domain is the whole inflected word including case suffixes/postpositional enclitics. Example diacritics in the quote are approximated from the scan (Hanke uses superscript i and dotted g/n letters).
new_statements.identity_note: Hanke describes the language of Bongu village (Astrolabe Bay, Konstantinhafen), into which the remnants of Gorendu and Gumbu villages had merged by his time; this is exactly Glottolog bong1291 / ISO bpu (Miklucho-Maclay's 'dialect of Gorendu-Bongu-Gumbu'). The appendix Sungumana vocabulary is a different language (Songum, snx) and is not the subject of the accent statement.

Akzent, par.10-11 (p.13): no fixed stress rule can be set up; of 196 polysyllabic words roughly equal numbers were stressed on the ultima and the penult, 25 on the antepenult, so the language prefers the last two syllables as accent bearers; accent shifts toward the end when a suffix is added (ingi 'food' > ingiga 'for food', bagala > bagaleo); in reduplicated forms the accent stays where the simple word had it (ole > oleole). Also p.84 par.145: yes/no questions mostly marked by intonation ('Betonung').
